utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think the best plan is to complete the hearing we started yesterday sometime later today, probably towards the end of our session and to carry on with the videolink arrangements now. So who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is General Aleksandar Vasiljevic by your decision only in relation to his written statement. So it will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please focus on Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you clearly. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for returning. You previously gave evidence and before you gave evidence you made a solemn declaration to speak the truth. That declaration continues to apply to your evidence today. You will now be cross-examined briefly by Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, good morning. I apologise for this situation, but it wasn't up to me that I had to call you again. My brief question is on the 25th of July, 2007, did you give me a statement, 2D387 that I will now show you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I did make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My second and last question is would you have made the same statement now and do you abide by everything stated in it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic, and I'm sorry for bothering you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That completes my examination, Your Honour. And I would tender the statement into evidence 2D387.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, do you have cross-examination or are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We completed our cross the last time Mr. Vasiljevic was before us and since the only other issues raised have been this new statement we have no questions regarding this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, do you have questions? Mr. Vasiljevic, you will now be asked some further questions by the Prosecutor Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, General. I just have a few questions --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- for you in light of what is in your statement, Exhibit 2D387. In your written statement that was introduced into evidence last January, and this is Exhibit P2600, and I would refer you specifically to paragraph 80 if you have that document there. And in English it's about six lines down in paragraph 80, and you're referring to General Pavkovic. The English translation -- I'll wait until you tell me you have it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please? Which paragraph in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 80, 8-0.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's the 6th sentence it which -- or sixth line which says: "He invited me to stay for dinner and said they were going to have a meeting of the Joint Command. His exact words." Is that accurate? He used those words, "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I know what may appear to be a problem at first glance. The expression "Joint Command" was used. In the course of the statement I gave to Mr. Fila it is written a meeting of the joint staff. I think these are finesses at what is the staff and what is the command. In actual fact, this was a meeting of the Joint Command which was used as an expression everywhere. I don't know what the problem is, whether one says Joint Staff or Joint Command. Anyway, it was a meeting when I came to the command of the Pristina Corps, and this meeting was held. And that was when the expression "Joint Command" was used, but I don't think there is any real difference between staff and command. This is just a linguistic finesse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your new statement 2D387, you say that Mr. Sainovic did not issue any particular orders. He listened to all the presentations and then briefly agreed that things should be done as planned by the generals of the MUP and army." I want you to look at Exhibit P2862, which is the excerpt from your diary of that 1 June 1999 meeting. Do you have that in front you, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go to that, Mr. Hannis, the transcript does not show and I didn't hear who you said made that statement, "He invited me to stay for dinner."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh. Your Honour, earlier in his statement that is referring to General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Pavkovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find that exhibit, General, P2862?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last entry is translated in English as: "Sainovic tasked them with action to be completed within three to four days." Do you recall what that was about --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- or -- okay. Could you tell us what that was? Is that what he said or is that ...

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I would first like to point out that what is stated in my work notebook is not a record or a minutes of the meeting, nor did I know that a meeting would be held. I always carry my work notebook with me, and as I had it on me on that occasion, I simply briefly jotted down what was said at that meeting. So I don't have a complete minutes, and the oral statement I gave to the best of my recollection is much more detailed than what is written down in this notebook. And I said that Sainovic gave the task that the operation should be completed in three or four days, and this was after the statement and briefing by General Pavkovic, what had to be done the next day to achieve better coordination of the operations of the units on the ground and that the people who had abandoned their position should be called to task. And this wasn't in the sense of any record-keeping. I simply noted down that the activities had to be completed to clear away Drenica or Jablanica. I'm not quite sure which but anyway the area that was discussed at the meeting. That's as much as I can say about what was noted here. I assume that the whole problem is he gave the assignment. I explained in my statement that I do not know what the official position of Mr. Sainovic was at that meeting. I described him as the most senior officer who enjoyed respect by all of us who were there. We stood up when he walked in, including myself. Now, whether he was the commander of a joint staff or a Joint Command, I can't say. I can just say that he was the most senior person by the positions he held in the government and a man of unquestionable political authority. That was my impression of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you if then reading your prior statement, P2600, and the new exhibit, 2D387, together, am I correct in understanding then that the generals described the operations that they planned to carry out and at the end of that Mr. Sainovic said that should be done within three to four days. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, accurate. That's what I noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the Witness, Your Honour. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you have cross-examined the witness. That should be the end of the matter with Mr. Hannis's re-examination, unless there's a particularly prejudicial development in the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am now in a dilemma. What is the statement that the witness abides by? If he still abides by what he wrote down, then I'm finished. I have a feeling that Mr. Hannis is undermining the credibility of the witness. What he did was cross-examination, not me. If you're showing him one document and then another, that's cross-examination. And he's undermining the credibility of his own witness, so I don't understand that. I just wanted to ask him one question. Does the witness abide by his written statement or not. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I'm just trying to clear up what's on the face of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that but what do you say to the request to ask that one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't object to that. You're the ultimate deciders. I was unclear on this because he had originally been a Prosecution witness, then he's listed as a defense witness and they put it in a 92 ter statement. I want him to be here for cross-examination on that statement and not let it come in by itself, so I guess he's his witness now, I cross and he can redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The confusion arises because the issue is one that was raised in examination when he was a Prosecution witness, and his status has not in theory changed, but the presentation of that document creates a practical difficulty that we understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we will allow you to ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic -- Mr. Vasiljevic, do you have the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please read out paragraph 4 aloud and tell me do you stand in every respect by what is stated there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He's already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's not the question you were going to ask, Mr. Fila. We authorised you to ask one particular question, and that's the question you should ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is it, whether you stand by the statement you have given in every respect. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your answer to that question, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do stand by the statement I made, and I believe that it is no different from the statement I gave during my testimony in The Hague. The question is whether a task was given or he agreed that things should be done as the generals had planned. The substance hasn't changed. It's a different way of putting things. Mr. Sainovic was the most senior person at the meeting, and when the meeting ended he said work should be done as planned, and the plan was to clear away the terrain within a period of three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. That was all I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, that completes your evidence and should be the end of it for you. I don't anticipate you being recalled again. Thank you for returning to assist us. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Zoran Andjelkovic, but I see that his chair -- I'm sorry, not Zoran Andjelkovic, Zoran Mijatovic, but I see the chair is empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand he'll be there momentarily. While we're waiting on the witness coming, there are two things that we could perhaps deal with. The first concerns Mr. Lukic and Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic, you made a filing about the expression "raised," and when we initially considered it we thought, suspected that you'd perhaps acted rather hastily and by mistake and you might wish to reconsider that filing. It seems to us a quite inappropriate thing to do at this stage in this case. We appreciate the debate that went on but the issue was one to which I and all my colleagues were alert and the point that you make is a fairly obvious one for submission in due course, and you then seek a blanket remedy in relation to objections in the course of the case which seems to us potentially frivolous. Now, we wondered if you might wish to withdraw this of if you wish to insist on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the blanket admonition, that part I think I will withdraw. However, if -- what -- what -- the reason I -- I too thought whether I should raise that point or not with respect to the misuse of the terminology, but seeing as how both I as a native English speaker still had to look up the terms in the dictionary to verify and Mr. Stamp also is a native English speaker misusing the term I had to I think make sure that the record was clear with regard to that and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But surely, surely that's matter for final submission and not something we should be batting back and forward across the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Then if that's the Court's position as long as that's reflected in the record I have no problem resolving that matter at the stage of submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do you wish to withdraw this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The other matter I can deal with at the moment is that after the winter recess we will resume sittings on the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour I thought you said the 16th. It comes out on the transcript as the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's just getting the best of both words, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect a small round of applause concerning your last statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please stand while -- while you make the solemn declaration. Would you now please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document you now have in your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Fila on behalf of Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mijatovic. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fila. I can hear you fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since we're talking the same language, after I finish my question could you make a brief pause so that the interpreters can catch up. That will make our work proceed faster, although it will seem slower.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell me first of all your name and your qualifications.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Mijatovic, and I have a law degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you worked and what duties you had in the MUP or, rather, in the State Security Service until your retirement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I started working in the State Security Service in the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia in 1970, and I started my career as an intern, as a trainee, rather, and I ended it as the assistant to the chief of State Security Service, Jovica Stanisic, for counter-intelligence so when I was retired on the 1st of January, 1999. Among my major functions in the State Security Service - I will not go into all of them - I started as an operative and then I was a branch chief, the chief of State Security Service in Belgrade, the chief of Intelligence Administration and my last post was the assistant to the chief for counter-intelligence and as I indicated earlier I retired on the 1st of January, 1999, at my personal request.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point you were recalled to service and then you retired again at your personal request. What was your duty during this brief period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I returned to the service on the 26th of January, 2001, and I was the deputy chief of the state security department. I retired again, but that was not on my personal request. In November 2001 I resigned to Zoran Djindjic's government that was in power at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And since not all of us know what this is all about, could you tell us in brief what is the sphere of activity of the State Security Service, and in particular in the first part of your service there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the State Security Service in its essence was the counter-intelligence service, and up until 1990, until the introduction of the multi-party system, in assisting to its counter-intelligence work it also dealt with the internal enemy counter-intelligence protection which was of particular importance for the defence of the Republic of Serbia, then counter-intelligence protection of various persons and analysis, background checks, things like that. And then after 1990 when the multi-party system was introduced the service did only counter-intelligence work, intelligence work, and work aimed at countering internal terrorism. So that would be in brief what the service did between 1990 and 2001 when I left the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your service did you ever meet a person by the name of Ratomir Tanic, and does he have anything to do with your service, the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I met Ratomir Tanic, I think, now I can't be really very accurate, between 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was his contact while you were in the service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Ratomir Tanic had for years collaborated with the State Security Service, even at the time of the single-party system. He was used in activities aimed at the internal enemies, and then Tanic got in touch with the foreign intelligence service and of -- he was then used as a collaborator of that service, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He got in touch with the British counter-intelligence service and he was used then as a collaborator of that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who were -- who was his immediate contact apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just correct you. I was not Tanic's contact. The operatives of the service did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you give us a name perhaps or would that be classified?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Maybe we can do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go into private session for that, because we're dealing with those kinds of services now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tanic receive any money for his services? What do you know about that, how much he received, from whom, when, and why?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The first larger amounts of money Mr. Tanic received came from the service. I think that was in 1993 or thereabouts. The assessment at the time was that Tanic's motive for working with the service was of financial nature, and when we decided to give him some money, since that was his motivation for his work with the service, we decided to make a secret document documenting this first payment, larger payment, and then later on if there was any lack of discipline on his part in his work with the service, we could then use it against it and bring it into line, as we say. This money that we paid to him was not too big in terms of what agents receive both in our country and in abroad, but given that we were under the sanctions at the time, the comparable amount would be 20 or 40 average monthly salaries. It was paid in hard currency, in German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your evidence before -- in his evidence before this Tribunal, Mr. Tanic said that he held a high rank in the State Security Service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: There were no ranks among agents in the service, State Security Service. Collaborators could be useful or not useful, could be trusted or not trusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Checked or unchecked but there were no official ranks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we have a reference to where in the record Mr. Tanic said he had a high rank?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will find it later. He said that he got promoted or advanced as his work progressed. That's what he said. But I'll find -- I'll find the reference and then if I find it I will share it with you. Because I can -- I can rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I would like the question rephrased to reflect the record, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's put it this way then: What was Tanic in the service from the beginning until the end?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that he was used in our work against the English service, and he was double agent, in our parlance. We didn't trust him. We used him to double-cross the English service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. What was his reputation in the State Security Service? I mean Mr. Tanic's reputation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: He was a man we didn't trust too much, and he was a man to whom we applied secret surveillance measures, secret measures of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, how would you assess the value of the information you received from him? Were they correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, after all those years I can't really make an assessment of the value of the intelligence he provided. He probably from time to time supplied some valuable intelligence, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it true that the information he gave to you would be at Slobodan Milosevic's desk within an hour or two hours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what was -- when the intelligence received by the service, by the head of the department, would find itself at President Milosevic's desk. That is not something that I knew. I didn't know anything about the communication between the department chief and the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But how could the department chief get the information from Tanic since you said that he had his contact, the gentleman that we called contact? Would it have to go through you or what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The department chief would get the information that would be classified. It would be marked Rabin, that was his code-name, and then there would be the actual report. For supplying the intelligence to the outside of the service, nobody could know the identity of the person supplying the intelligence. Even the department chief did not have to remember the identity of all those agents, and he would sometimes perhaps ask who is this man? I don't recall that he ever asked anything about Tanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us make our question simple. Did Tanic get instructions from Jovica Stanisic through you or did he send intelligence through you to Stanisic which would then be at Milosevic's desk within an hour or two hours? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's complete nonsense. That's not how the service functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did Mr. Tanic get instructions through you or from you and you in turn from Stanisic and Stanisic in turn from I don't know who to establish channels with Western countries to improve Serbia's relations with them? Did you ever give him such instructions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error "Stanisic"] Tanic was a small-calibre agent. My most recent book, "Ambush for Serbs," gives you a very good idea of the actual calibre of all of our agents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. It says here Stanisic was a small-calibre agent. It should read Tanic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Tanic. Tanic was a really, really small-fry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You can give me shorter answers, yes or no answers. Is it correct that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the State Security Service authorise Mr. Tanic through you to negotiate about the settlement of the Kosovo crisis until 1998, in the time period leading up to 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The service did not have any power to do that, so that would be just Tanic's confabulation, and he was prone to such flights of fancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it correct that during those purported negotiations you often met with Tanic and that he had a direct link with Slobodan Milosevic through you? What would you say to something like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I never had any direct contacts with Mr. Milosevic. I don't know anything about those purported negotiations that Tanic may have participated in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The answer to the first part of my question, were you very -- did you meet with him very often about those contacts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just tell you one more thing. I met Tanic five times in my entire life, and he received his instructions that were related to our game with the English intelligence service, and I will not be going into that because it has nothing to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's correct, it doesn't. Mr. Mijatovic, is it correct that you told Tanic that a secret annex had been signed in Dayton allowing NATO to get all the information it needed about the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yet another nonsensical statement. I have the entire Dayton agreement with all its annexes in my possession, and there was no such option provided for in the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that's not what you said.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how could I have said it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have to apologise, Mr. Mijatovic. I'm not asking those questions. I know the situation, but is it true that Tanic through you at the beginning of 1998 already, but -- informed Milosevic but through you that NATO would attack if the operations in Kosovo continued? That is apparently a report he got from his sources.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and explain as briefly as possible the year 1998. From April I became assistant chief of the department of counter-intelligence, and from then on my jurisdiction towards the collaborators of the Belgrade centre ceased. That means in April. So I saw Tanic for the last time in December 1997. As for NATO's intentions, we had very good collaborators, and you can assure yourself that I'm telling the truth by looking at my book "Ambush for the Serbs," which -- from which you can see when the bombing of FRY was concerned that the sanctions were just changing what had been planned in 1992, and in 1997 and 1998 we had very precise data as to what was going on. You can check with the book. I didn't prepare myself for this just now. But Tanic's information was very low-level. He never had any such information. We had very precise and very reliable information through our intelligence agents primarily in the West.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it true that you and Tanic together came to the conclusion that the tactics of the Serbian police in Kosovo was first to send a few policemen to a particular village for them to get killed while special units were already ready to destroy the whole village after that? Is anything like that possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot comment on the logical and moral nonsense that this implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you ever tell Tanic that Sainovic was actively involved in provoking the war in Kosovo? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it true that you passed on to Tanic the information that Sainovic was carrying personal messages from Milosevic to Kosovo and that those messages were in contradiction with the situation on the ground and that they were illegal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a reference to the course of this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is again nonsense. I'm unaware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have references for these two propositions that you've put, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can be of assistance, if I may. For the previous question it is page 6325, 6326; then page 6332 up to 6340 of the transcript. All these questions being put by Mr. Fila are contained in those pages of the transcript, and you will certainly recall that Tanic's testimony was rather confusing so it is very difficult to pinpoint a particular sentence but it is contained in these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said that Tanic said this. I'm asking whether the witness said this to Tanic. I think that is the proper way for me to put the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand, but Mr. -- yes. But Mr. Hannis's suspicion is that you're asking that question because of something Tanic said here when he gave evidence, and he's seeking references to the pages where Tanic dealt with these areas, and Mr. Petrovic has been good enough to give us these, and if Mr. Hannis is unhappy with that, no doubt he will tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've just looked at the first reference, Your Honour, and it does indicate Mr. Tanic is answering a question and says: "I don't have direct information from Mr. Sainovic about that, but I have very reliable information from the State Security Service." He didn't say he had information from this individual in particular. So that's my -- that's my complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me have a look at that. Are you talking about page 20, line 2? Or 19, 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me find it, Your Honour. I'm looking at line -- I'm looking at line 20 -- I mean line 12 on page 20 where Mr. Petrovic said for the previous page it's 6325.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but is that in relation to the question at 20, 24, or the question at 20, line 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that was the question at 20, line 2. Well, actually, it touches on both. I'm looking at the transcript from 10 November at page 6325.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if -- if he says he has got information from the State Security Service and we have here a member of the State Security Service, it's surely legitimate to ask him whether he passed that information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. My concern was the suggestion that he's the only source of Mr. Tanic's information for the security service and I don't think that was his evidence. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't see anything wrong with what you're doing, Mr. Fila, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it true that you told Mr. Tanic that Sainovic in 1998 obstructed the work of the State Security Service upon orders from Milosevic so as to create -- create the situation -- the impression that the situation in Kosovo cannot be dealt with in any other way but by means of war? Did you tell him anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic and the service in those days had no contact as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you have said something like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: How could I have when we were completely independent? We didn't depend on Mr. Sainovic or on others. Of the service was headed by Mr. Stanisic, who was the chief of the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's quite difficult to control the situation whether there might be an objection in this context, Mr. Hannis. So that I get the picture clear, that question was very specifically about what this witness might have said, and it does appear to presuppose that Tanic gave that specific evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Initially I was going to object to the question that starts at line 2 on page 22 where he says is it true you told Mr. Tanic X, but his last question in formulating that question was did you tell him anything like that? Now, I don't have a problem with the question phrased that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But is it true you told him is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the answer to my last question was yes or no, because there's a problem in the transcript, that you informed Tanic that Sainovic obstructed the work of the service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it true that you spoke to Tanic about many problems that you had with Sainovic and that Sainovic had improperly interpreted information coming from Milosevic down and from the bottom up towards Milosevic, that you told Tanic this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what information Slobodan Milosevic received.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But did you say anything like this to Tanic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: If I don't know what information he got, how could I say that? After all, Tanic was our agent. He received instructions for his work from us. So it was not up to us to inform him, but it was up to him to inform us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What you are saying is that the information went from him towards you and not vice versa.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. And as -- let me repeat once again that his main area was with the British intelligence service. And after all, in 1999 he was engaged by them as a witness in The Hague Tribunal, and he started working for them. So that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, did you say anything or is it my poor recollection about Tanic being a double agent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say that he was a double agent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And with that knowledge would you perhaps misinform him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. That is customary when dealing with intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you ever say to Mr. Tanic that there is a tape recording of a conversation between Sainovic and General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I hear that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This brings me to the end of my question. Is there any possibility that you may have said any of these things to Tanic in order to mislead the British intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. What we did regarding misinformation of the British intelligence service is something quite different. It's not linked to the topic of criminal acts of which the accused Sainovic is charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Witness. That is the end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does any Defence counsel wish to examine? I see no one indicating an intention. Mr. Hannis. Mr. Mijatovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Hannis, the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mijatovic, can you tell us who were the personnel in the Ministry of Interior in 1998 and 1999? We know who the minister of the interior was. Can you tell us who the deputy ministers were that were in charge of the RDB and the RJB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, that is until he was replaced, Jovica Stanisic was the head of the State Security Service, and the assistant minister and chief of the public security service was Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when was Mr. Stanisic replaced in his position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That was at the end of October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Obrad Stevanovic, and, if so, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what position Obrad Stevanovic had in 1998, but I do know that he had a senior position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the RJB; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about a man known by the nickname Legija? One name I've head for him is Milorad Ulemek, but I believe he has another name as well. You know who I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. He was the commander of the Special Operations Unit of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that unit is sometimes referred to as the Red Berets or the JSO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know where we're going since I'm testifying about Tanic's statement. I don't mind answering your questions; I just don't understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, there is no limitation on the areas that counsel can explore in questioning you as long as they are relevant to this trial, so please answer any question Mr. Hannis asks unless we instruct you not to. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you also know David Gajic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a colleague of mine, and he was also the assistant chief of the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what position did he hold in relation to Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: He was assistant chief of the State Security Service of Jovica Stanisic, and he coordinated the work of the State Security Service in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with the JSO, who was -- who was the commander or the overall head of that unit in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 I was retired, and until -- that is, in 1998 I know with reliability that the commander of the unit was Milorad Ulemek and the person responsible for that unit was Frenki Simatovic, who was also assistant chief of the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware when you returned to your work in 2001 or thereafter did you become aware that -- that there were allegations that the JSO had committed crimes in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That the JSO had committed crimes in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, when I returned to the service I did not know that, but what I did know was that individuals had taken part in other acts of crime, and as a service already a month later we arrested the perpetrators of the crime on the Ibar highway. So what we knew, we took action against and started prosecutions. As for this fact about Kosovo is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you weren't aware of any allegations about crimes committed by JSO members in Kosovo and in particular regarding Dubrava Prison in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I think I have to object. I believe Dubrava Prison or Istok has been removed from the indictment. We've discussed this time and time again and we've not had evidence led would respect to this, so I don't know why we're going into this at this stage unless we want to restart this case from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It goes to the credibility of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall repel that objection. The -- no attempt is being made to explore the facts. What Mr. Hannis is seeking to explore is the witness's knowledge in relation to his credibility. So please continue, Mr. Hannis. It would be better, I think, if you were to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, my question was, were you aware of allegations that JSO members had committed crimes in Kosovo, in particular at Dubrava Prison, in 1999. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Today at page 12 you told us you returned to the service on the 26th of January, 2001, and then you retired again in November -- or you resigned. Why did you resign at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I handed in my resignation after the protest of the JSO unit against the arrest of Banovic brothers and their extradition to The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the Banovic brothers were associated with the JSO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The Banovic brothers are people from Bosnia, and they were demanded by The Hague Tribunal on charges of crimes committed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But wasn't part of the reason for your resigning in 2001 because the JSO in effect was staging a sort of rebellion or revolt against extraditing the Banovics to The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: My resignation was based on political manipulations in connection with the protests of the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were the protests of the JSO about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The fear was that the new leadership of Serbia would surrender all people requested by The Hague Tribunal and accused of crimes would, in fact, be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was the new leadership headed by Mr. Djindjic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the leadership of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who in particular?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: It was Goran Petrovic and all of us who still had senior positions in the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But isn't the matter of handing individuals over to The Hague Tribunal a matter for the government and not for the service? Or was the service running things in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: We are the operative organ or the executive organ of the government, and that leads to our duties and obligations, and we acted in accordance with those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure you answered my question. Are you saying that if the service didn't want to find or arrest fugitives, then they would not be extradited to The Hague? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: Who made the decisions about whether or not fugitives or indicted individuals would be handed over to The Hague? Who made that decision in your country at the time of 2001? Was that the government or was that the service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The government made the political decisions, and we put into effect those political decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And part of this dispute was the JSO did not want to be handing over individuals to The Hague Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly that's correct. They sought the support of certain political factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You told us that after 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you departing from that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because I don't understand it. You referred to: "Goran Petrovic and all of us who still had senior positions in the State Security Service." Now, what are you saying about him and yourself in that connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was that in the previous period when Rade Markovic headed the service and Nikola Curcic and when we had the previous system, that is the period from 1998 until 2001, the indictees of The Hague Tribunal were not extradited. That was the political position, and that was how the police acted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was your fear --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just meant to say that we -- at the time Jovica Stanisic was the chief, at your request we did hand over Erdemovic, who was put on trial here. I can't remember the second person who was also handed over for -- charged of war crimes, and we took to trial the Vuckovic -- Becko -- Buskovic [as interpreted] brothers. Also in 2001 we passed on to The Hague Tribunal in accordance with your rules documents for criminal prosecution of the KLA, and we also prepared documents for the trial of persons who took part in the kidnapping of the 17 Muslims from a bus in Serbia. So I'm saying that the Markovic [as interpreted] leadership did take specific measures for the perpetrators of the worst crimes to be found and handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But -- but was your fear that Petrovic and you and others might be arrested by the new government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What government are you referring to, sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm completely -- I really don't know what you're saying was the reason for your resignation. You talk about political manipulation. That's meaningless to me. I'm just trying to be clear about why it is you say you resigned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying that. I handed in my written resignation, and it was published in the media, and you can see it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just you tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What should I tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hopefully, the truth. Why did you resign in 2001?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Fine. Well, I don't know if you have enough time, or should I perhaps give you an abridged version of what actually happened in 2001 when we were talking about the rebellion of this unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A very short explanation of your reason for resigning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Several days before the rebellion we had handed over the Banovic brothers to your Office of the Prosecutor. They were charged with serious crimes committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After a few days after their arrest, the unit rebelled. I don't recall the exact date, but it was in November, and on that occasion people who led the rebellion made two basic requests that led them to actually rebel. One was that there should be no more arrests or surrender of people to The Hague Tribunal before the law on cooperation with the Tribunal was enacted because there was no such law in place at the time, and the second demand made by the rebels was to remove from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me stop from there. Just tell us why you resigned. Did you disagree with them? Did they force you out? What was the reason for you resigning? We don't want the whole -- I don't want the whole history of this. I just want to know why you resigned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You see, inside this bloc that came into power after the toppling of Milosevic there were some political disagreements primarily regarding the cooperation with the Tribunal. We encountered first problems within our service after Slobodan Milosevic was surrendered, and those rifts continued. And after this unit rebelled, there was a political -- big political rift regarding the policy of our cooperation with the Tribunal. Dusan Mihajlovic, who was the interior minister at the time, used this rebellion for his own ends. That was the main problem for me. And ultimately nobody from that government stood up to protect the service that had done its job in accordance with the demands made of it by the prime minister, Mr. Djindjic. Nobody would be in such a state service if they did not get the support of their own government for the kind of work they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, you've written two books that I'm aware of about your experiences in the service; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the first one is translated into English as "Requiem for a State Secret," and the most recent one this year is "Ambush for Serbia." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We just got that most recent one days ago, as far as I'm aware, and I don't read Serbian and we haven't had an opportunity to translate it all into English, but I understand in that book you write about this JSO rebellion and your reasons for resigning in that book, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm talking about in both books.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Among many other things as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, ""Requiem for a State Secret"" is exhibit P2915; "Ambush for Serbia" is P2917.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I will come back to those in a few minutes, Mr. Mijatovic. I have some questions on those, but I want to ask you about [Realtime transcript read in error "Mr. Stanisic"] Mr. Tanic. Today at page 14 you've said that -- well, first at page 13 you said you met him - you couldn't be very accurate - it was sometime between 1992 and 1993. Did you not keep any kind of records in the service about when you first met him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at page 33, line 17, my colleague Mr. Hannis asked a question about Mr. Tanic and the record reflects that he asked about Mr. Stanisic. Perhaps that could be corrected so that any confusion is avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mijatovic, the question is about Mr. Tanic. Can you deal with that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Within a single year I have about -- between a thousand and 2.000 contacts so it is very difficult for me to recall this contact that I had with Mr. Tanic, when it was exactly. It was not of any great importance and I wouldn't be making any notes of it. The notes are kept by the operative. I was there with the operative, but I was not making any kind of record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the operative would have made a note of that first contact with Mr. Tanic, and that would be in the records of the service; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those records should still be in existence and available; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what you mean when you say every records. The records of the operative actually contain information about his contacts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Records of the agent actually contain information about his contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. When you say records of the agent, are you talking about the person who works for the service who had had a contact with Mr. Tanic? Is that where the first contact by Mr. Tanic would be noted in the service's records?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the operative writes a report about the agent or collaborator. I don't know what was recorded by the operative at that meeting with Mr. Tanic, whether he recorded the fact that this was the first time that I met him, but I did not write a report on the agent. The operatives did that. I cannot, despite all my willingness to do so, I cannot tell you what was written there because I don't know it, but at any rate, the agent report would indicate that I was present at that time during that contact, and if I had made any suggestions to Tanic as our agent it would be recorded there and also the type of suggestion that I made. That would be definitely written in this report on agent code-name Rabin. I don't know recall whether at that time his code-name as Rabin or not. I remember for operative reasons his code-name got changed at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you returned from the service were there any limitations put on you or did you sign any kind of agreement that you would not reveal secret information you had learned in the course of your employment with the service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. On my return? Are you talking about the time when I returned to the service?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Isn't it standard procedure in agencies like yours that when somebody retires they -- they sign some sort of agreement or promise or commitment not to reveal the information that they were privy to as a result of working for the service? And perhaps it would help if you would look at Exhibit 2922. That's a document that the Registry officer should have there for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We don't have it in English, Your Honour. The ERN is 0611-1937.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a statement. It's signed. "I hereby undertake that in accordance with," and so on, "Official secret," and so on. It was signed on the 12th of January. I can't really read the date here. The 12th of January, 1999. Yes. That's the 12th of January. That's when I retired. It was signed at that time, and I am happy to say that I have not yet reached that area where I would be revealing any state or official secrets. This is something that you have to sign before you get your first severance payment or first pension or, rather, your first severance payment because you get your pension later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying that none of the things you wrote about in your two books fall under that prohibition? Both those books contain a lot of details about individuals and events and things you learned about in the course of your employment at the DB. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I did write about the notion of state secret, what I thought about it, and what happened to us after all those years with the state secret, because we're now in a totally absurd situation regarding all the things that are considered to be -- are classified as state secret, official secret, or military secret. This is what I wrote in my first book. The authorities of the Republic of Serbia did not consider that in writing my first book I actually revealed any of the state secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: And the first book is actually just a response to my contacts with the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal and their improper behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how do you know that the authorities did not consider what you wrote in your first book to be revealing state secrets? Did you ask any permission ahead of time before writing your book about putting those things in there? Did you get any kind of waiver?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I did not seek any such thing, but do you think that I revealed any state secrets?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you're in a better position than I am to know what is a state secret for the republic of Serbia, but I'll ask you some questions about that in a minute. Let me go back to Mr. Tanic for the moment. At page 14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that--

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Hannis, 2922 will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 14 today you were talking about payments to Mr. Tanic in answering Mr. Fila's question. You said "the first larger amounts of money Mr. Tanic received came from the service. I think that was in 1993 or thereabouts." And you said: "When we decided to give him some money, since that was his motivation for his work with the service, we decided to make a secret document documenting this first payment, large payment, and then later on if there was any lack of discipline on his part in his work with the service, we could then use it against it and bring it into line, as we say." What sort of secret document are you referring to there? Just something showing how much was paid to Mr. Tanic on a certain date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to apologise, but in order to clarify things and to give you a more specific answer to your question, the previous question concerned secrets. I would never talk about Mr. Tanic as an agent or a collaborator if he had not indicated that he had been our collaborator in his testimony before the Tribunal. Regarding those documents that relate to Mr. Tanic and the operative who was his contact, we had lunch at Usce restaurant and we recorded the actual payment, the changing, the money changing hands, the hard currency that was used with concealed cameras. I think it was about 2.000 German marks at that time, so it was not a very high amount. So you can gauge his value as a collaborator. But this amount was high if you take into account the fact that we were under the sanctions at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That was the average salary in Germany at that time. Mr. Tanic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. We didn't hear the witness because of shuffling of the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the last part of Mr. Mijatovic's answer didn't get recorded, and that was that Mr. Mijatovic -- that Mr. Tanic was not aware that he was being recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's what Mr. Hannis was about to clarify with him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, you said about 2.000 Deutschmarks. I think when you testified earlier you said that was the equivalent of 20 to 40 months of salary in Serbia at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was the amount. At that time sanctions were already in place, and the effects began to be felt, and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then I'm a little confused because you just said "It was not a very high amount so you can gauge his value as a collaborator." Twenty to 40 months worth of salary, two to three years worth of salary, is a significant amount, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everything is relative, but I think that no intelligence service in the world pays its agents 2.000 German marks. I would like you to tell me which service would do that. I don't think that any service would do that. We paid some of our more valuable agents more, the agents that we trusted more and whose intelligence was of vital importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in 1998 -- 1997/1998, let's say, how -- well, I guess in fairness, let's go back to 1993. In 1993, how many of these kinds of agents was the service paying? Was it 10? Was it a hundred, a thousand? How many are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I'm giving evidence here, I would not like to be inaccurate. You're now bringing me back to a time that's 14 years ago, and I wouldn't like to mislead you in any way, but I think that that was not his monthly salary. That was the annual salary. I'm talking about the Belgrade centre. I can't tell you anything about the rest of Serbia, but there were some agents who would get more than he did, but those were not huge amounts in German marks. So I think that some people would get about 7 to 8.000 marks. I allow for that possibility. I'm not talking about the Belgrade centre. That's the caveat. There were other centres in Serbia, but I don't have any information as to how much their agents were paid, and I don't want to mislead you in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you can't tell me how many agents were being paid, whether it was 10 or a hundred or more; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the exact figure now. I served for 30 years in that service, not three days. I worked with the operatives and agents. I was the head of the counter-intelligence service where people were paid in a different way. I was the head of the Belgrade centre, so I could perhaps get a little bit confused. If we are talking about 1993, I can't give you -- I don't know how many agents there were, but quite a few, I would say. I can't give you the figure. I don't think that it would be fair of me to just give you a figure now, and it would be difficult to check whether it's accurate. Dozens of them were in contact with the Belgrade centre, but as I said, there were some agents who were leftovers from the single-party system where we did some other kind of work. We had to deregister some of our agents, to find them some shelter because some of the things that we did in the single-party system we could no longer do in a multi-party system, so we had to restructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get a rough idea because you've tried to tell us that Mr. Tanic was a very small-fry in the hierarchy of agents. How many agents were paid 7 to 8.000 marks, which might have been as much as 80 to 160 months worth of salary? How many of those big fish?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing, in 1993, that was the year when --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Could you just answer my question. Please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether you want to really be able to understand my answer. At that time we put the stress to intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, the reasons for having them are not being asked of you. The question is: Roughly, roughly, how many agents were paid 7 to 8.000 marks in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993 in Belgrade centre. That's what you're asking me about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hannis will be happy with that for a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: A dozen or so approximately, if you're insisting, but this figure could be greater or smaller, but that would be for intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to note that, and that's a very important thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a suitable time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I address the Chamber for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that I don't make any objections about the time, but please bear in mind that I have a third witness to examine, and videolink is limited in time. I took 25 minutes to examine my witness, and the Prosecutor has already taken 45 minutes, and judging by the documents that he indicated he would be using, he would be asking him questions for two days. I have a third witness, and I would really like to examine him too. Could he please stick by the regulations, by the provisions for the first two, and then I will not insist for the third one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will -- there's a lot of material with this witness that relates to my case. It's not limited to just Mr. Tanic, and under the rules I understand the cross-examining party is permitted to go into those areas that relate to his case. I'd like to do that. I understand the time constraints. I'll try to go as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the overarching provision is that generally the cross-examination should be confined to the time for examination-in-chief, but where there's good reason then it can be extended on the basis obviously that time will be made up elsewhere so that the overall picture will not become distorted. There plainly were occasions when Defence cross-examination far exceeded examination-in-chief, and the reasons for that were explained at the time. Mr. Hannis's indication is that there is much in his own case that he feels it appropriate to explore with this witness, and we consider that that is an appropriate reason for extending the time. We're also conscious of his undertaking to be as brief as he can. You also know, of course, Mr. Fila, that you have the videolink arranged for tomorrow and Friday as well, so there is plainly ample time to deal with this. We are conscious of the problem, and we're --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I hear of it. I wasn't aware of the fact that we would have a videolink arranged for tomorrow. I was told that we would have videolink only for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's not the information I have. Perhaps that can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There appears to have been some miscommunication, Mr. Fila. Because of the number of applications made, arrangements have been made on the assumption that the evidence could spill over, and the link will be available tomorrow. Now, hopefully that will be sufficient, but if it's not, for some reason it will also be available on Friday, but we're not anticipating now that that will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm absolutely sure that I will end today as I anticipated. And Mr. Prosecutor may call Mr. Mijatovic, just as I did Mr. Vasiljevic, because I brought Mr. Mijatovic here to challenge evidence by Mr. Tanic, and that's why I need him. But if the Prosecutor needs him for this or some other case in some other respect, then he may call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the practice we follow here, Mr. Fila, and I can't at the moment see on what legal basis in the system we have the Prosecutor could be calling witnesses at this stage. He has to cross-examine witnesses called by the Defence to deal with any issues that he feels are necessary -- it's necessary to explore, and therefore he will be allowed to continue and hopefully if we don't debate the matter for too long we'll make fairly rapid progress and perhaps achieve a compromise solution for both. We'll now break and we will resume at 20 past. Mr. Mijatovic, the Court now has to have a break, and it will be for just under half an hour on this occasion, and we will resume at 20 minutes past 11.00. You can take a breather while we have this break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, we'll continue now with the cross-examination. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, you've described that one time you made payment of money to Mr. Tanic and you video recorded that without his knowledge. Was that the only time that he was paid money by the service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was not the only time, but I think the other occasions were linked to special occasions, the new year, for instance, and they were much lower sums. I don't know what they were exactly. Because we would reward all our collaborators on such occasions, so I can't remember, to tell you the truth, how much he may have received, because this was not something I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where in the records of the service would that information be found, the total amounts paid to Mr. Tanic during the time he worked for you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules of service which were in force at the time I was there, when cooperation ceases with a collaborator all documents relating to that collaborator are destroyed. So my answer is nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to a question from Mr. Fila at page 15 today, you mentioned at that Mr. Tanic was a double agent, that you didn't trust him, and, "We used him to double-cross the English service." And double-cross is sort of a standard operating procedure in your profession, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say exactly when from the standpoint of our rules and procedures he became a double agent. I can't tell you when that was, but I know that this must have been roughly in 1997, if I can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you told us before that the last time you had contact with him was December of 1997. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Now let me see whether it was December or January. I assume it was one of those two months, but not later. We did have telephone contact, that is Tanic and myself, through a third person who was the contact. We did have telephone communication through this contact, and then he completely went over to the British side, and then I got in contact with the British agent, Mr. Busby whom we had processed when he came to Belgrade and who tried to bring me with Tanic to Vienna for consultations, and I later realised that this was connected to my testifying in The Hague Tribunal. Of this with Tanic misled Busby.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You've gone beyond answering my question, and if we can try and focus on my question, just answer the question we'll get done sooner. You mentioned that you had telephone contact then after December 1997 or January 1998 through the third party who I take it is the person you named in -- in private session. An operative who worked for your agency was the person who was speaking with Mr. Tanic by telephone; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And up until when or for how long did that go on? I guess -- let me ask it this way: When did you decide that Mr. Tanic had gone completely over to the British side? When was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I said probably at the beginning of 1997, but I cannot claim with certainty that it was at the beginning of the year, but there is a high degree of reliability that this was a person who was in contact with the British intelligence service and that with -- in relation to us he's not absolutely sincere. Now, this is a professional issue which should take a lot of time if we were to discuss it, and I'm sure you don't want that. In 1999, because of suspicion that he really is not sincere towards the service, the security centre arrested Tanic. He was given certain assignment. After that, he went abroad and took the other side, and I think I have said enough, that he simply went over to the other side. I think that's quite clear. I don't think anything is in doubt to that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He went --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: He never returned to the country again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He went abroad in 1999 after -- that was after he and his wife were arrested, if you will --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: After the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- by the JSO. They basically kidnapped them off the street, didn't they? Put bags over their heads and held them for three days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: He was not arrested by the JSO but the State Security Service. The JSO was acting upon instructions for the operatives. The operatives of the State Security Service arrested him. There was an interview with him to clear up his relationships with the British intelligence.
