He was given certain assignments, and with the approval of the service he went abroad and he stayed there, and then he appeared in The Hague Tribunal, as we all know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you write about that in your book "Requiem for a State Secret," don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you write about it in your second book as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I may have referred to it in a sentence or two. Not about Tanic, but I didn't discuss Tanic himself in the second book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's in your first book, and I'm looking at an exhibit, an excerpt from your book which is Exhibit P2915, and there's a chapter or a section called "Mihajlovic's trip to Paris." Do you recall writing about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in October 2001 Dusan Mihajlovic who had previously been head of the New Democracy Party was the minister of interior for Serbia and your boss; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that chapter you talk about an October 2001 trip Mr. Mihajlovic took to Paris where he met and spoke with Mr. Tanic. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me read you a little portion about that and you tell me if this is an accurate translation or at least is consistent with your memory. You say: "My French friends gave me the details two days after his return," meaning Mr. Mihajlovic. I take that you're referring to other secret service or French secret service operatives who gave you the information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to my personal friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And they just happened to know the details of the meeting between your minister, Mr. Mihajlovic, and Mr. Tanic? These are just casual friends who know the details about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: This was unofficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who do those friends work for?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: It was just due to circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who do those French friends of yours work for?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: For no one. They're my friends. Does a friend have to work for someone?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they paid by you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I said they were my friends. Maybe the interpreter is not interpreting properly. You know what a friend is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sometimes friend pays -- friends pay friends for doing jobs for them. Did you pay them or did your service pay them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I do not pay my friends. And I would like to ask Your Honour to intervene. I consider this to be pressure on me during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question's very simple, Mr. Mijatovic, and you've answered it. I doubt if you're going to be asked it again. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of these two friends? And we could do that in private session if you want.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot. My friends are more important than anything to me. To betray a friend is like betraying one's homeland. That is my life's motto.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is betraying a friend more important than your oath to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I am telling the truth, but friends are friends, and I don't want to put them in an awkward situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question was: Is betraying a friend more important than your oath to tell the truth here now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I am telling the truth. My friends informed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said you cannot tell us their names. You mean you will not tell us their names; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I told you what my principle in life is. You're linking friendship to something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking about payments and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking, sir, is because I'm having a difficult time understanding how two friends, I guess it's at least two, friends of yours, French friends, happen to know about a conversation or details of a meeting between the Serbian minister of interior and Mr. Tanic, who was at that time sort of on the run. How would they happen to be in a place where they would know the details of that meeting and that conversation? Can you explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, Tanic and Mihajlovic were not alone during that conversation, and I continue to say that it was due to circumstances. There were several people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Including your friends.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the other people present who were not your friends?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now whether it was Djordjevic, Petrovic, and I don't know who else. Goran Petrovic. The Chief of Cabinet, Djordjevic, the owner of the restaurant, the personnel, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I assume -- I assume, then, that this would be reflected in the records --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: This was in a public place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I assume there's some kind of report or record of this meeting in the service archives; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what you wrote in the book is based on what your friends told you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go on with the rest. I'm sorry we got side-tracked. You said: "True, several months before, Mihajlovic had asked me about Tanic, his relationship with the RDB, disagreements with the service at the time of the NATO aggression." And then -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you go on and say: "I told him as much as I could, that he was an agent of a foreign service and of our own, that he worked for money, that he was a bad man, and that I would check what had been happening during the NATO aggression." Is that correct? That's what's in your book.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you say: "I checked and said he had cheated. Scores are settled somewhat differently in times of war. There were kidnappings and beatings, and his wife had been kidnapped." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: All that is correct. That's what I was saying a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you go on and say: "I realised another important thing. He had been kidnapped by members of the JSO." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: But not for their own needs, but for the needs of the operatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware that Mr. Mihajlovic has written a book about his experiences, including some of his experiences while a minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you read that book?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to another item, and I'll come back to that. You said that you met Tanic five times in your entire life. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I said a few times. Now, whether it's five, six, or four, I'm not sure, but somewhere midway would be five.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, at page 18, line 11 today, you said: "I met Tanic five times in my entire life." Was that correct or you're not sure now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Five times -- I didn't count. You're attaching significance to this. Fourteen years later I'm trying to assist. You're insisting on this number. As far as I can recollect, for example, five times, because really I didn't keep any records or minutes, and 14 years later, in view of the fact that I had up to 2.000 contacts a year, five times is all right, if the number means anything, but it is certainly a single-digit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. All right. In answer to one of your questions from Mr. Fila about whether you conveyed certain information to or from Mr. Tanic, you said: "How could I have when we were completely independent? We didn't depend on Mr. Sainovic or others. The service was headed by Mr. Stanisic, who was chief of the service." And that's -- you recall saying that today? That's at page 22, line 10. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's an accurate reflection of the attitude of the State Security Service, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. Could you clarify the purpose of that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you don't need to know the purpose to answer the question, sir. Doesn't it reflect the attitude?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The service was headed by Jovica Stanisic. Work instructions were received from Jovica Stanisic. Never during my 30 years of service, and especially for these 15 years, did I receive any instructions from Slobodan Milosevic or any politician of the day, not a single one, nor was this possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But why was that not possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That is how the service was structured. It was a multi-party system. Jovica Stanisic did not allow us to get into any kind of contact with the leaders of the political parties at the republican or local levels. The policies of the service were in the hands of Jovica Stanisic. We didn't have any direct contact with the political authorities, as far as I am concerned. I can't guarantee for others, but the head of the largest centre in Serbia, as the person who headed the Serbian intelligence service for a time, and as an assistant of Jovica Stanisic, I did not have any contact with politician from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in your position you are aware, aren't you, that Mr. Stanisic had a direct line to Mr. Milosevic? Even though he's the head of the service for Serbia, he had a direct line to Mr. Milosevic, President of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they maintained contact, nor can I talk about it apart from what I wrote in my book when we had two protocol visits to Slobodan Milosevic and which I covered in detail. But work instructions, tasks did not come from him. The method of communication between the head of the service and the president of the republic or other politicians is something I am not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me return for a moment, because I did find my note about Mr. Mihajlovic's book, and let me tell you what he says about the meeting with Tanic and you tell me whether that's consistent with your knowledge of that event. He says, and I'm reading from -- the exhibit number is P2916, and the English excerpt is for -- is at ERN K 053-8559. And I'm reading page 5 of that. He says: "The next time I saw the ill-fated Tanic was only after 5 October, and this was in London." Now, in your book you say it was the 1st of October in Paris. Were there two meetings or does Mr. Mihajlovic have it wrong, or is one of you changing dates and places to misinform readers? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I do not wish to interpret the minister of the interior. As far as I can remember, I don't think I said the 1st of October. I may have said a date in October, but I don't remember saying the 1st of October. I don't even know whether I went into the dates. You have it before you, so you can check. I would rather not comment on what Mr. Mihajlovic said. I stand by what I wrote in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then he says that Tanic told me about what had happened, and he said: "He and his wife were abducted by some people wearing balaclavas who put plastic bags on their heads and held them somewhere for three days and nights. With the bags on their heads the whole time they were subjected to the worst possible forms of physical and psychological torture." Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I have partially read the conversation with agent Tanic, and this exists in writing, so perhaps it would be best for you to get hold of it so as to avoid me giving any rough estimates. It was not the JSO who talked to him but the operatives, and there's a detailed report about this and you can ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: This report? You mean the report about the interview with Tanic in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned an agent Ganic. Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I saw it in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know the agent's first name so we can try and locate that report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There were several operatives talking to him. I just looked to see what the topic was and why he was kidnapped. Only when Tanic contacted me to establish telephone communication with me through a third operative. Then I looked it up to see what was happening because I thought it was strange that he wasn't in the country whereas the political circumstances had changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Petrovic up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the impression that there's some confusion here, that in the question of Mr. Hannis, 56, line 3, an agent Ganic is mentioned. I didn't hear the witness mention any such name. I think there is a confusion with the name. Perhaps Mr. Hannis could check. I don't think the witness mentioned any Ganic. It's probably Tanic and not Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I thought I heard Ganic, but I see in the transcript that it is agent Tanic. So thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I was mistaken about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, let me ask you about -- maybe this is what you're talking about. I'll skip down a couple of paragraphs, and this is again from Mr. Mihajlovic's book. He says: "When I came back to Belgrade, I requested a report from the service about this. I cannot cite details from this sensitive report, but I can say that the service put the Tanics through hell because they were cross-checking the games he had played with them." Is that a fair characterisation of the report you recall reading, that the Tanics were put through hell?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, when someone says to put someone through hell, I don't know what they mean by that. I would not like to try to interpret what is said here. It's best if you read the report. Of course when one writes a book of this kind, one tries to be dramatic. I probably did the same in my first book. The books he wrote and the book I wrote, they are not court documents. One should draw a distinction between literature and statements made in court, and unfortunately here we are dealing with literature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, it will probably come as no surprise to you that there can be difficulties from time to time in locating documents that could assist the Court from the archives in Belgrade, and therefore it's perfectly legitimate for counsel to explore your personal recollection, and he wants to know if what you read could be described as putting that couple through hell. Now, would you care to try and assist us more specifically than passing the buck to the report, which we don't have access to at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really wish to assist. I just said that the description putting someone through hell, it's a matter of opinion. Of course they were not gentle with him. I'm sure he was put under pressure, even physical pressure, that's certain, but it wasn't torture, I think. However, the way he was brought there was very unpleasant. We were in a situation where our country was undergoing airstrikes. I would simply have arrested him in the street. I wouldn't have used those methods. But whether it's putting someone through hell or not, I can't say. Of course it's unpleasant. When you're brought in by the police in times like those, especially as this was a double agent, there must have been physical contact as well. There might have been beating, I don't know, but I really cannot say anything precise about this because I wouldn't like to mislead anyone. If you are interested in this clarifying interview, as it's called, you might try to find out what the service thought of him at the time, why they were settling accounts with him in that way, what sort of tasks he had and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, was his wife mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. I know she was brought in, but whether she was mistreated or not, I really don't know. The situation in itself is an unpleasant one. It is linked to much unpleasantness. I am not saying that it was something normal or necessary, but I cannot interpret the actions taken by the then leadership. I want to distance myself from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but bear in mind we're looking for your recollection of a report which someone has described as indicating in the report that the couple were put through hell. Now, is there nothing in that report that you remember about how she was treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe we do not agree about the report. There is some confusion concerning Mihajlovic. In the service there is a report on the whole action as regards Tanic and the contents of the interview. To the best of my recollection, and I'm really trying to be helpful, that report about the interview with Tanic is about 20 pages long, and he was interviewed about everything he had given the service up to that point in time. Suggestions were made as to what he was suspected of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please simply deal with the question. Is there nothing in that report that you remember about how she was treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it said that. I don't think it said that. I cannot remember that anything was written down about the wife or how she was treated. It would be almost incredible if they were doing something bad to her that they would write it down. If someone used illegal methods, of course they wouldn't put that in the report. I don't believe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess that ties in with the point that I wanted to get to later, but now is as good a time as any. Misinformation is something that was a way of doing business for the service; correct? Isn't that something you do in -- in state security work? You use misinformation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's not the essence --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things, Your Honour, two points. First, the witness already answered this question when you asked him this. For an hour and a half this witness is being cross-examined, and my examination was only 25 minutes long. That's not fair. The Prosecutor cannot put questions for as long as he likes; otherwise, I cannot tell people how long their testimony will last. The rule is that the Prosecutor should take as long as we take. Of course we can tolerate some discrepancies, but I have never seen in any trial and this is my sixth, I think, that the cross-examination should take so much longer than the examination-in-chief. That's how I organise my time. That's how I organised in the case of Kesic. You said we should be brief. But this takes us into all kinds of territory, and there is a limit somewhere. I have to organise my case. I want to complete it. I apologise for reacting like this, but now the Prosecutor is repeating Your Honour's question. Your Honour's put the same question. We are wasting time. My time is also being wasted. Well, we have to draw a line somewhere. If I examined for one hour, he can examine for two, but tell me so and then I can organise my time accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, it is generally the overall time used in evidence that's crucial, and that applies in more than one way. You will have whatever time you need to re-examine this witness on the various matters that the Prosecutor has raised that you did not deal with in examination-in-chief, but we consider that the cross-examination so far has been directed to a very important issue in this case, and therefore it's one of those circumstances in which there is good cause for extending the period available to the opposition to cross-examine the witness. As I explained to you earlier, Mr. Hannis will have to find ways of making that up at a later stage in the overall calculation of the time that's being used, to be fair to everyone. But when -- and if there's any indication that he's -- he's straying off issues that are relevant to the trial, then he will be stopped, but at this stage we're not prepared to do that and we'll allow him to continue. We do however, agree that the question he's just asked has been answered and he should move to something more specific. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, a couple more references to your books, and this regards access to documents. The report about Mr. Tanic and his wife, if you were trying to find that document yourself, it was about your wife and your family, and based on your experience and knowledge of the service where would you go to find that document? Where would that be kept? Who would I talk to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That document, I assume -- I can only assume as I have no contacts with the service now, I would look for it in the BIA, in the section referring to the British secret service, and I'm sure it would be found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in your -- in your book, your first book, "Requiem for a State Secret," I think that's at page 169 in the B/C/S. It's in chapter 17. And this is Exhibit 2915. Chapter 17 is about meetings with Hague investigators in Belgrade and Skopje. And the draft translation I have says that you were denying the ICTY access to DB archives, which is consistent with your supervisor or your boss, Mr. Petrovic's view which is quoted as being: "This is why Serbia went to war with the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. We're not going to have investigations or searches of our archives, not while I am the chief of the department." That was -- that was his attitude and your attitude then about the ICTY having access to the service's archives; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: You have read it all. It was our standpoint that without the permission of our state organs, our archives were not open to anyone who wanted to come in. Our archives were available, as we demonstrated to you when we handed over to you 64 files about the KLA crimes in Kosovo. We also had cooperation with individual investigators when Severin was at issue, abductions, and other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: One couldn't just come in and say, "Give us the documents." We had our rules --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: -- and our legislation to comply with. If there had been no cooperation, Milosevic would never have arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you about another page in that book. Page 182. You are talking and say: "I had some discreet conversations with N. Sainovic in 2001. I will not reveal what he said. It would not be correct towards him or towards the truth, towards the history." Will you tell us now what those conversations were about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you had read the entire passage the question would be superfluous. You're probably aiming at something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can't read Serbian.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: You should have taken the whole passage relating to Mr. Sainovic. This includes his standpoint on the Hague Tribunal. As for the rest of our conversation, it was a man-to-man conversation about his family, his personal tragedies, and so on. And I'm a very discreet person. If you continue reading you will see that Mr. Sainovic also touched on the topic of The Hague. He was on the list of those accused, and after the abduction of Milosevic he said it would be good if a law was passed on The Hague, that he was aware that he had to go to The Hague but he wanted to go there in a legal manner. He felt that the way Milosevic went there was illegal. And I think it says in another book that he even gave me a draft that the Socialist Party had done. It was a bill on a law on cooperation with The Hague. I didn't put it in the first book. I think I did put it in my second book. And I gave that draft to Mr. Djindjic, and I said, "Prime Minister, Mr. Sainovic is sending you this as a sign of goodwill because some things should be made legal with reference to The Hague." And Djindjic's opponents wanted the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about why you left your job the first time in 1999. What was the reason for leaving the service then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 Mr. Jovica Stanisic was replaced and the -- Rade Markovic became chief of the department and Nikola Curcic became his deputy. In the meantime I heard that he had died. On the arrival in the service they made some staff changes. Even after the dismissal of Jovica Stanisic I remained assistant chief of the counter-intelligence department, but this was just on paper. I just carried out part of those tasks formally. I was dissatisfied because two men who were not from our department had been appointed and they did not have a good reputation within the service. Previously we had had information about Rade Markovic's close connections with the Milosevic family and his connections with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, please. Mr. Fila's anxious that we get through this and that you're not kept longer than necessary. It would have been simple enough for you to say that you were unhappy about the way you had been passed over for promotion. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, I want to ask you about something that David Gajic said about that transition when Mr. Stanisic was removed, and I'm looking Exhibit 29 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just a moment. The witness is trying to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it you're trying to say, Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no ambitions. I left the service because I knew what sort of men these were and where they would lead the service. What they did in 1999 and 2000 confirmed in the worst possible way that I was right in my decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now you'll see how easy it is to create the wrong impression if you go into detail that's quite unnecessary. Thank you for that clarification, but you could have equally given that answer in one sentence. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Court and counsel, I'm referring to Exhibit P2914, which is an ICTY statement of David Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, you -- I see Mr. Ivetic standing up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm shocked to find the Prosecution would actually refer to this exhibit which I think the Court is somewhat aware of the history behind it and we are in the process of doing a motion for sanctions relative to the same. Just to refresh the Court's recollection, we asked while Mr. Gajic was alive for any indicia of the interviews conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor with Mr. Gajic. The Office of the Prosecution advised us that no such evidence in written form or in recorded form existed of the interviews after Mr. Gajic died, and indeed after this case had been on for one year. Then the Office of the Prosecution in response to our motion to bar contact with witnesses at that point in time gave us for the first time a 27-page signed statement of Mr. Gajic that they had just conveniently found coincidentally at that point in time which was just given to us recently and which of course we have been unable to undertake any steps to verify and therefore I would object to the use of this exhibit based upon those grounds and the failure of the Prosecution to adhere to the rules, in particular Rules 66 and 68 with respect to giving us this material in a timely fashion so that we may prepare a defence. And if they were going to be introducing this exhibit into evidence now, I would strongly object to the same and if need be I can have a motion for sanctions abbreviated and filed later today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this statement was taken in connection with the Haradinaj case, and this was one that we did not find when we did our searches before the trial started. The only thing we had found was that there had been an interview with Mr. Gajic on another occasion on which the tape recording did not work and no statement was written. Upon doing our updated searches for witnesses we discovered this statement, and we turned it over to the Defence as soon as we discovered it. I have no further explanation at this time. I know that the search was done for Gajic and any materials related to him on more than one occasion, and it was only on this most recent occasion that we found this statement in our records.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, we still have not been given the notes, recordings, et cetera, for this particular interview. My request was very specific with respect to any and all recorded material from any interviews of Mr. Gajic. I was told none such existed and now despite having no records of any interview existing, we have a signed statement. I don't know how a signed statement is created if there are no interview notes, recordings, et cetera, all the other materials that I had sought. And the only reason this motion has not been filed, we are trying to find the actual response from the office of the Prosecution that delineated exactly the response to our very specific and very broad request with respect to Mr. Gajic's interviews that occurred over many days with the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things that continues to puzzle me here is why parties always find it necessary to preface questions by reference to a statement which in itself won't be admissible as evidence in support of their case unless the witness agrees with the propositions in it, and why these propositions cannot be put without specific reference to the statement is difficult to understand. If all you're doing, Mr. Hannis, is giving the Defence an indication of the source but you intend to formulate questions for the witness to deal with that don't depend on the reliability of Gajic, then why don't you just do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess it's the practice that I'm used to where I need to have a good faith basis for asking my question and by indicating where I am -- where I'm drawing it from, I'm trying to indicate to counsel why I'm asking the question and why I have reason to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there's a difference between the stand-alone value of this statement, which at this stage will be nil, and the value of anything the witness says having been prompted by the statement. In light of that, do you still maintain the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As long as the Prosecution sticks to what they've just represented, I think we're fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to complete this and without asking for any further response, it does seem to us, Mr. Hannis, strange that such a specific request could be made for material and that because that material related to the Haradinaj case, it wasn't located for this case and wasn't passed on. We find that a difficult situation to understand. It would be much more relevant, of course, should the Prosecution have sought to admit the statement of Gajic as evidence in the case. However, for the moment please proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, would you agree with the -- well, first of all let me ask you this: Were you aware of anybody, any organ or body or committee called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- were you familiar with a group of men, including Mr. Minic, Milomir Minic, Mr. Dusan Matkovic, and Zoran Andjelkovic, who were sent by the SPS to Kosovo in the summer of 1998 to try and deal with the problems there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't engage in those activities. I was assistant for counter-intelligence in the State Security Service. I heard about this for the first time in the courtrooms of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: About those three gentlemen going to Kosovo in the summer of 1998? This is the first time you've heard about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I was not involved with Serbian or Montenegrin politicians in those days. I engaged in counter-intelligence. As to reports whether a politician went here or there, I could have read in the media, but they were not the object of my activities. Foreign intelligence services were my concern. That was my main preoccupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1998 wasn't one of the biggest threats to Serbia the possibility of an attack by NATO because of things that were happening in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I did deal with those things, and you can read about that in my second book in great detail in fact. I delved into the NATO bombing and everything else related to that. I don't know what these four gentlemen have to do with the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your -- in your assessment, isn't one of the reasons that Mr. Stanisic was removed from his position was because Mr. Milosevic was not pleased with the information that the RDB in Kosovo was providing him about the situation there? Isn't that one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what all the reasons were that prompted Mr. Milosevic to renounce Jovica Stanisic as the leading figure of the service. In my first book the"Requiem for a State Secret," I did speak of the 30th of July, 1998, of a meeting that was unexpectedly called by Mr. Stanisic, and you can find this in the book, and he said that the situation in Kosovo was getting out of control, and I quoted this in the book, that the unruly behaviour of the police could no longer be tolerated. I remember his statement, and I also remember the following, if I may be of assistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, if you'll stop now because you've answered me question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: -- that the service --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you another one. Were you not aware that Mr. Stanisic himself attended at least one meeting of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in the summer of 1998? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me assist you. I do not know that such a command existed nor did Jovica Stanisic report to me, because in a service such as ours it was me who briefed Mr. Stanisic and not the other way round. I was not aware of the daily schedules of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about Mr. Gajic? Did you have any working relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: With Mr. Gajic. Let me see, the 27th, the 28th -- 29th of October, 1998, when on assignment from the chief of the service I came with Mico Nikolic to carry out security duties stemming from the agreement Holbrooke-Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That doesn't seem to answer my question. With David Gajic did you have a working relationship?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I had only this one contact with Mr. Gajic and that was when I came to carry out security and counter-intelligence activities in accordance with the peace agreement signed by Holbrooke and Milosevic. I may have seen Gajic for an hour or two during my work. You can find that in my book so as to save time. No other contacts. Let me add that the day I reached Mr. Gajic in the afternoon at 5.00 Stanisic was replaced so that the whole thing was linked to that. And the next day I continued doing my work, which had nothing to do with Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had Mr. Gajic already been removed by the 1st of October from his position as the RDB coordinator in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I think not, because he was there when I arrived. He was there, and he was doing his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your book "Ambush for Serbia," you talk about intercepted conversations between US diplomats Holbrooke, Hill, et cetera, and conversations between General Mladic and General White. Are these intercepted conversations that were made by the service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I have attached a document of the conversation between White and General Mladic in order to show the absurdity of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, please listen to the question and answer the question you're asked, which is whether these intercepted -- intercepts were made by the RDB. It's yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found those documents in a safe box. It is coded. So I assume these were documents prepared by the service as there are no markings on the document. Mladic's document is dated 1993, so it is 14 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when and where did you find those documents?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: About 10 years ago, one of them, and this one, in 1998. I don't remember who the source was, who gave me the document. The other one -- as for the one 10 years ago, it's difficult to remember. The letters were unusual. You will see in the book. It is an attachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm confused now. You said that somebody gave you one. Before, you said you found them. Can you tell us where you came into possession of these documents?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Which one are you referring to, the first document about Mladic? That was 10 years ago. I found it somewhere. I don't know, among some papers I received. How I received them I can't remember. I received daily about 200 documents, so 10 years ago it's difficult to be precise. And I also cannot claim who drafted it. Some other service --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: -- which is not excluded. But I do wish to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. And you kept that document --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: We get -- I'm sorry. We do get hold of documents that foreign services have as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you keep that document for 10 years so you could write about it in your book?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Is that relevant for what I'm testifying about today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believed that the Serbian people need to know everything that was going on during the last 15 years, at least how talks were conducted with Mladic, how they prepared themselves, how they set the targets, how Holbrooke ordered that the insignia be removed. I was aware of what I was doing, but I believe that if The Hague may open certain secret documents, then I, too, may open certain documents to see the other side of our misfortunes, and I stand by what I said. If that is the topic of your examination, I will be glad to explain all this in even greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So isn't it a fact, Mr. Mijatovic, that the way you operate is if you feel it's appropriate or important or necessary, then you're willing to provide misinformation, to lie, to do whatever you want? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I have never lied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, is that correct, sir? Let me refer you to your book "Ambush for Serbia" at pages 40 to 42, and you admit lying three times, including two times to your minister of interior, Mr. Mihajlovic. Isn't that correct? That's in your book. Is that just fiction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: You need to read the whole text. You are now trying, and I understand that, to challenge my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you answer my question? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I have answered. What I write and what I wrote the "Ambush for Serbia," this is literature. When I talk about the minister, it is with a certain measure of humour. So you cannot use something that is publishing fiction, you can't use it in court. I understand your purpose, but I'm quite at ease, and I am an honest man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So let me get this straight. Are your books then sold as fiction or is it supposed to be real-life biography?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: It is not a biography. It is publicistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. Mijatovic. Mr. Seselj made a filing in his case entitled "Addendum to Motion for Trial Chambers to Investigate Contempt Proceedings." This is Exhibit P2927, and in that he attaches what purports to be a statement from you. If goes on for several pages, I don't know, 30 or 40 pages. Do you recall making that statement for Mr. Seselj to use?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see what the Prosecutor is talking about? Will you tell us what you're talking about, please? Could the witness read those 40 pages? He can -- if you're giving him so much time, he can go on reading until the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to know if you refer making such a statement for Mr. Seselj. It's quite lengthy. You don't recall having done that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do this for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh. But you did make such a statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, let's have the date and let's have an indication of the document for the witness so that he can deal with it specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Exhibit P2927, and it was made in Belgrade on the 12th of April, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does that help, Mr. Mijatovic? About three months ago.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please ask me the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need to tell us if you remember making the statement first of all. Do you need more information before you can answer that, or do you remember making this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember this statement, but the way in which the Prosecutor is putting the question, I don't understand. I didn't make any statement to Seselj. As far as I know, Seselj is in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just for the sake of being accurate on this, Mr. Hannis, you should put to him to whom the statement was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, on the document itself, Mr. Mijatovic, there is a certification or a verification which says: "This is to certify that Zoran Mijatovic signed this statement in person and confirmed the signature on this document as his own." It was verified using an identity card issued by the Belgrade MUP. I guess that's your number. At the 3rd municipal court in Belgrade on the 12th of April, 2007. Do you remember having given such a statement? Maybe not to Mr. Seselj or for Mr. Seselj, but about the events in -- in Serbia and in connection with your service.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, if you had put it that way, it would have been easier. I did make such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally, did you also -- were you involved in an investigation involving a transfer of approximately 900.000 Deutschmarks from Mihalj Kertes to Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I personally took a statement from Mr. Sainovic according to the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, could we register how many hours the Prosecutor used in his counter-examination? I didn't have that right when it was the case of Prosecution witnesses. I also have another statement to make. If I had known there would be a videolink tomorrow as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assumed -- I'm sorry, I did assume that he would organise this, but I didn't know that this was explicitly organised, so I apologise if I said that I didn't know. I know there was the intention, but I didn't know whether it was organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the time is available, Mr. Fila, but what do you mean by you didn't have that right when it was the case of Prosecution witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every time I was told how much time the Prosecution used and we shared out the time left for us. Your Honour, I'm not opposed to anything that is being done, but the rules have to be the same for everyone. I plan my time. Believe me, it is very difficult. I don't mind that he took so long, but I should have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should read the terms of the orders we've made about time, which clearly allow for situations where additional time is necessary. However, please continue with your re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mijatovic, Mr. Mijatovic, a lot of time was spent on establishing the value of 2.000 German marks and why you said that this was the equivalent of 20 to 40 salaries. You mentioned the sanctions. Will you tell us what the salaries were in Serbia in those days because of the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that in those days, as head of the Belgrade centre, I barely received 50 or 60 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many dollars is that? Because it is more understandable here.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: It must have been about 50 or so dollars.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Secondly, as you were involved in counter-intelligence, were they using those German marks to spend them abroad, not in the country?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that particular case when he received 2.000 German marks we were preparing him to work with another intelligence service, and this included costs of petrol, hotel accommodation, et cetera. So that the profit he himself made would be about 500 or 600 German marks. So he didn't have such weight that he would receive that sum every year. This was just an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mijatovic. I apologise for having kept you so long. It was not up to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, the reference to 50 or 60 German marks or dollars was for what period of time working? Is that for one month or is it for one year or what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we received our salaries in two parts, on the 1st and the 15th of the month. So my half in 1993 was about 50 plus 50, but I think, though I'm afraid to be specific, everything is measured very precisely, but I think after a year and a half of sanctions that salary was even lower, even though I was assistant chief of the service. We had a very difficult time in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do I correctly understand that you got about a hundred Deutschmarks per month?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this was the beginning of 1993. The -- the situation became even more disastrous as time went by during the sanctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, when you were asked whether your book was an accurate biography or fiction, you said it was not a biography but you gave some description of it which was not recorded on the transcript here. Could you say again what it was that you offered as the description of your book?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I said it belonged to the genre of publicistics or journalism. It's a book that uses some biographical data and certain documents to tell a certain story. My book is linked to my interviews with The Hague investigators and I explained why, and the book wanted in a specific way to talk about the war crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia to bring those events closer to the readers. The second book that I wrote was prompted by the bombing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This was certainly an action by the world that the world will not take pride in and I wanted to show the other side that the public was not aware of and that was the intelligence aspect of those events. What we as a service sent reports to the head of the service and the head of the service to our political leadership. That was the idea. Of course this is not a document. This is not a testimony. This is publicist writing when a certain degree of freedom is allowed, as opposed to something called biography, court records, or a statement according to Law on Criminal Procedure. This is a literature and that is how my books were evaluated officially by historians and politicians. With the first book I had no problems. I did not have any negative comments. I had good assessments by the director of the institute for criminology, the historian Markovic, and others. Let me not enumerate them all. I had quite a lot of conversations about this, media reports and interviews. Unfortunately, I was dealing with a very serious problem and from the standpoint of you sitting at the bench it is viewed differently and I can understand that, but I'm telling you what my idea was. A book can be read in different ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was put to you that on pages 40 to 42 of the book you say that on three separate occasions you did lie and one of these was to the minister Mihajlovic. Are you saying that's accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: It is a work process that is involved, a communication that is clear to everyone, and I'm really sorry, Your Honour, that you did not understand the nuances from the book. This is a humouristic thing and this was read in the Serbian parliament and met with laughter by the deputies, and I'm sorry that you didn't gather the irony of this. I'm really very sorry. I'm sure you have much more serious work to do than read my book. This has nothing to do with my credibility. This is just a remark, a relationship with the minister of the interior. We had a specific relationship and sometimes when he asked such things of me I couldn't refuse, but I would joke with him. I would do the job, talk to the people and so on. I don't think it is a good idea to focus on an excerpt which has nothing to do with the things being discussed here which are of the greatest importance. I think we've lost a great deal of time over such matters. If you were to read the whole book and the context of the story, you would see that this was just a decent measure of irony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have not had the opportunity of reading the book, but we shall be reading the bits that have been referred to and, if necessary, the context in which the book was -- or these passages were written. So we will take account of what you say when we look at these various passages. Thank you very much, Mr. Mijatovic, for coming to give evidence. That completes your evidence here, and you are free to leave the room in a moment. The court staff beside you -- the court staff --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your patience to hear me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The court staff will now take your earphones from you but please stay where you are until the court adjourns in and minute or two. Mr. Fila, can you give me an indication of the length of time you anticipate being with the next witness, because you were much shorter with Mr. Mijatovic than we -- than we expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take less than an hour for the next witness. So please don't grant the Prosecutor a week. I intend to complete my case on Friday, so can the gentleman organise his cross properly, and I will do so as briefly as possible, because this is what you requested of us, and that was a good example, the way we did Kesic, and then we hear the cross for four hours. But never mind. I'm joking now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anger doesn't last long with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could you give us an indication of how long cross-examination is likely to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: An hour. I'll be shorter with this witness than I was with Mr. Mijatovic, I'm confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reason I ask is that we would like to try and complete the issue of the interviews of witnesses so that we when we deliberate tomorrow will be able to make a decision finally on it. Now, you have something more to say. How long is that going to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Less than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We'll probably then interrupt the evidence about 20 minutes or 15 minutes probably before the end of the afternoon session so that anything that needs to be said about the motion to bar interviews can be said and we can deal with it. So you have -- well, we will now be adjourning until 2.00 in view of what's happened, so you will have from 2.00 until 3.15 as a period for evidence and from 3.15 to 3.30 to deal with the motion. Court is now adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.57 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the next witness is Dusan Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Matkovic. Good afternoon, Mr. Matkovic. I heard no interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear him, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, can you hear me? Could you stand, please, while we administer the solemn declaration to speak the truth. Why are these things not resolved before we come into court? Mr. Matkovic, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which you are now holding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Fila on behalf of Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Matkovic. Will you put your headphones over your head, otherwise you will lose them. That's better now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: My name is Dusko Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. There was no interpretation of that question for some reason. Could you repeat the question, please, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, could you please tell us your name, your qualifications, and what your state party and economic positions you performed in 1998 to 1999. Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: My name is Dusko Matkovic. By training I have a degree in economy, economics. In 1998 and 1999, I was general manager of the ironworks in Smederevo called Sartid, and I was vice-president of the Socialist Party of Serbia in charge of economic issues, president of the economic council of the Socialist Party of Serbia, and I was a deputy in the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. As we speak the same language, would you please make a pause before answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In view of the positions you held, could you tell us what were the political aims of Serbia and Yugoslavia that were aspired for in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: The political goals of Serbia then and of course today as well was to ensure peace, stability, prosperity, economic development, and above all the safety and security of all the citizens of Kosovo for them to be able to live and work normally. Those were the main goals of the Socialist Party of Serbia and of Serbia as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that an important issue in those days in the party and among the state leadership?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Yes. It was extremely important. Not just in Serbia, I would say, but in Yugoslavia in those days, as it was called then, and it was prominently featured in the world media as well and in the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you explain now how you happened to be in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: In 1997 I went to Kosovo for the first time as the general manager of Sartid because we had three plants in Kosovo, and I went touring those factories, which was a part of my job, and in 1998 I went there as a member of -- shall I call it a party working group for Kosovo. I think it was on the 10th of June that we had a meeting of the Main Board at which, upon the proposal of President Milosevic, the Main Board took the decision and elected a three-member working group that was to assist in stabilising and resolving the problems which existed in Kosovo. So I was in Kosovo as a member of that working group of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this meant to show the interest the party had in the situation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: The Socialist Party of Serbia was not ruling party in Serbia at the time and the most responsible in the political sense for events in Kosovo, and it could not ignore such an issue but on the contrary gave it a maximum of attention. And I remember at that meeting of the Main Board this issue was discussed at length. Of course the president of the Socialist Party of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, chaired that meeting, and the introductory address was made by Mr. Minic. There were some speakers in the discussion, and it was pointed out that the number one issue, the most important issue, was the question of Kosovo to which we needed to devote the greatest attention, that all state bodies should take part in this, and of course that the party should assist as well, that of course the problem was so great that they couldn't deal with it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who were the members of the working group, and what was the role of each of them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: The members of the working group, in addition to myself, were Mr. Andjelkovic and Mr. Minic. And in view of the political involvement and our overall political experience, Minic was mainly in charge of political communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm interrupting you. Was somebody the leader of the group and others the members of the work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: I couldn't really say that there was a leader of that group. We simply worked as a team. Maybe Minic had more experience in politics than the two of us, but we functioned as a team, and our agreement as to what each of us would mostly focus on was that Minic should have political communications with the Socialist Party of Serbia and other political bodies in Kosovo, with the political institutions of the Albanians and so on, whereas Mr. Andjelkovic was in charge of fieldwork, so that everyday life should function properly, organisational issues, whereas I was primarily concerned with the economic activities in Kosovo, seeking to renew them, to keep them going, so that I was mainly in charge of economic issues. And that is how we worked as a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you aware whether state bodies of Serbia and Yugoslavia took measures for each entity within the frameworks of its jurisdiction should strengthen its presence in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Yes. Of course in view of the magnitude of the problem facing our country at the time, state institutions were involved in assisting to deal with the problem, and in that sense the government of Serbia had its own coordinator for those activities on behalf of the government of Serbia, and I think it was Mr. Andreja Milosavljevic, I think his name was, yes, Milosavljevic, that was on behalf of the government of the republic. On behalf of the federal government there was Mr. Sainovic, and I remember that the Foreign Ministry also had its own outpost in Kosovo, the Foreign Ministry, because of the large number of foreign representatives, delegations that were coming to visit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Among the persons you have mentioned and the groups that were sent to Kosovo, and you have given the reasons, was there any form of subordination? I'm referring to the SPS team, Minister Milosavljevic, the Foreign Ministry outpost, and Sainovic. Were you in any kind of subordinate relationships?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Absolutely not. No one was more important than anyone else. We each of us did our part of the job. Each of us was tasked to work either by the party or by state entities. So there was no subordination, and we sought to achieve the greatest possible degree of coordination in order to achieve our goal and that was to bring life back to normal, because at the time it wasn't normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the reasons that the federal government had in sending Mr. Sainovic to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: I think that in my previous answers I have already given part of the explanation. Not a single significant state institution could afford not to be present and involved in dealing with the problem, and I know that Mr. Sainovic, on behalf of the federal government, by decision of the federal government, which means by decision of the prime minister in the federal government, Mr. Minic [as interpreted], was dispatched to Kosovo to deal with the problems within the purview of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's an error in the transcript. It says Mr. Minic, but it should be Mr. Bulatovic who sent Sainovic to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was Sainovic in the federal government?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was the vice-president of the federal government in charge, primarily, of coordinating these activities in the field of foreign affairs. Of course he had other duties as well, but the bulk of his activity, to the best of my understanding and perception, and as presented to the public, was that he was the vice-president in charge of coordination and work in the area of foreign policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now referring to your working group, Minic, Andjelkovic, and yourself. When you arrived in Kosovo what was the situation like there when you arrived, especially the economic situation in the province?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: I have to tell you that it is very important for me briefly to tell you about a meeting that we first attended of the Provincial Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia, and I have chosen this intentionally as the first example I wish to tell you about, which means that the party we belonged to and the provincial party was the main body of the Socialist Party of Serbia and Kosovo. We had a meeting which was extremely well attended. I think it was in June. I don't know the exact date. The 15th or 20th of June. It was our first meeting down there. And this meeting evolved in a terrible atmosphere. Tension was extremely high. Members of our own party told us that we were inactive, that the state was inactive, that the situation in Kosovo was tragic, that communications had been blocked, that life is not normal, that children could not go to school, that they feared to go to the shops, that the KLA had simply taken over control of the situation in Kosovo, which was very shocking for us. I remember that meeting well. It is still very clear in my mind. Some very sharp words of criticism were addressed against the party and the leadership, including President Milosevic. So I wanted to illustrate how desperate the situation was. And then we were able to see for ourselves, being unable to visit a village between Pristina and Pec that was surrounded by the KLA, and the people were in a blockade. They were running short of water and food, and it was not possible to visit them. So our impressions were very bad. And from other discussions and information we received, we realised that the situation in Kosovo was, I would put it, dramatic. And of course we informed the appropriate persons in Belgrade about this when we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you mean your party or others?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: In the first place we had a conversation with the Secretary-General of the party, Mrs. Gajevic, and after that a meeting with Mr. Milosevic at which in a part of the talk we very frankly told Mr. Milosevic how difficult the situation was, and he realised not the seriousness but the drama of the situation which required measures to stop, halt this trend, and then to take steps to overcome that situation, to bring life back to normal in Kosovo, and to ensure normal life of both Albanians, I underline Albanians, and Serbs and Romanies and all others living in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the meeting of the -- at the meeting of the Provincial Board were there representatives there who were not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't recall now the composition of the Provincial Board. I have to say that there were between a hundred and 120 people there, and I think based on the composition of the Socialist Party of Serbia in general that there must have been representatives of other communities, not only of the Serbian community or of the Serb people in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Matkovic, could you please very briefly explain to us what was the activity of this working group that the SPS Main Board sent to Kosovo in the summer of 1998? So what was -- what were you, Minic, Andjelkovic, doing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Well, we first wanted to get as well-informed about the situation as possible, because being well-informed is the best basis is for whatever needs to be done afterwards, and then we operated up the political channels. We also coordinated activities with all the other relevant factors who may have contributed to an improvement of the situation in Kosovo and to achieve a peaceful settlement of the crisis. We took those political steps. We talked to all the political agents. We talked to the people. We tried to ensure them that we would take measures to stabilise the situation. We visited many, many places in Kosovo, a lot of the factories, some of who -- some of which were unable to operate at all. There were attempts to disrupt normal production in some of the factories, and we tried to achieve that those factories that were still operating to operate normally. I remember that there was factory in Vucitrn, a great factory. I tried to get special security for this factory because there had been several attempted raids in order to disrupt the production there, to frighten the employees, and so on. So our activities were primarily of political nature and of coordinating nature. This is what politicians are supposed to do in such a dire situation. And of course it was not the way that we would have worked in Belgrade under normal conditions. In Kosovo you had to be active. You had to work 15 hours a day. You have to call all of those people who might be able to assist, including the military and the police. And if you allow me, I would like to just tell you that immediately after our departure to Kosovo, soon afterwards, there was this terrorist raid, the terrorists from the Kosovo Liberation Army at the Bilacevac mine in the immediate vicinity of Pristina. We found ourselves in a completely unusual situation. And this crisis, I think, lasted 10 to 15 days. They held a certain number of employees hostage. I think at the beginning there were dozens of workers who were held hostage. Production was disrupted. Of course their objective, apart from the usual political goals of the terrorists, their effort to frighten the public, they also wanted to disrupt the supplies of fuel to the Obilic electrical plant, to disrupt the supplies of power, and the people in the surrounding villages were very frightened. We talked to them. We tried to it calm them down. They set up night watches because they were really frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. So you painted this picture for us. I want to ask you, at the time while you were there in Kosovo and Metohija as a working group, were there any meetings between various state bodies that were present there in the field of their representatives?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: You mean joint meetings of all the representatives of state organs or bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Well, to be quite precise, the main task of all those who were present at Kosovo at the time was to do their job, but there was a certain level of coordination. There had to be. We as politicians felt the need to inform representatives of the republican government, of the federal government, and the representatives of the military and of the police about what we were able to see, we as politicians, to keep them informed and to get some feedback that we needed for our political activities. So we initiated certain contacts. For instance, the first contacts were established in this Bilacevac crisis where we called the representatives of the military and the police. We asked them to give us information. We wanted them to -- we demanded that they do something, because that's what the people demanded of us because they were so upset. So we initiated a certain degree of information exchange and a certain level of coordination in order for our efforts to be better synchronised and to achieve better results on improving the situation, because there were abductions, rapes, murders on a daily basis in Kosovo both with Albanians and Serbs and others as victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, those joint meetings were held; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In order to ensure the exchange of information.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How often did those meetings take place? Was there a rule?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning we spoke with people on the phone mostly. Sometimes there would be a meeting but sporadically. We would meet with the representatives of the military or of the police. I guess that is what you're mainly interested in. But as the situation really deteriorated and became even more difficult a need was felt for this kind of daily communication. It was not on a daily basis but almost on a daily basis that we met. The daily news were every evening at 9.00 -- at 8.30 at the Radio Television Serbia, and we would meet afterwards, and then on the basis of daily events we would discuss the daily events, analyse them, and then decide what should be done later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat once again, because the transcript -- transcript doesn't really reflect that. You mentioned the daily news on the RTS, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MATKOVIC:
